title: Indra and the dream
hook: Indra's second try: the dreaming self, lit from within, still weeps
carry: the dreamer isn't the deepest self

segments.voice: Yesterday, Virochana took his reflection for the self, and Indra turned back. In the Mandukya Upanishad, the waking self is one quarter, not the whole.

Indra walked back to Prajapati, firewood in hand again, and said: the body can go blind, and die. That can't be the self. True, said Prajapati. Stay another thirty-two years. When the years were done, he gave a new answer. The one who moves about happily in dreams: that is the self. It made sense. A dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind, or lame when the body is lame. Indra set off home, pleased. And again, on the road, he stopped.
screen: `BACK AGAIN, FIREWOOD IN HAND.` → `THE DREAMER IS THE SELF?` → `AGAIN, HE STOPS.`

segments.voice: Because in a dream, Indra saw, the dreamer still suffers. It's as if it's being struck, as if it's being chased. It feels pain. It even weeps. That's no self beyond sorrow. He turned around a second time. The Mandukya gives this dreamer a beautiful name: taijasa, the shining one, from tejas, brilliance. Its fourth verse says the dream self knows inward and enjoys the subtle: images, memories, feelings, made of mind. Commentators explain the name. In a dream there's no sun and no lamp, and yet everything is seen. The dream is lit from within. In om, it's the second sound, u, between a and m, the way dreaming sits between waking and deep sleep. So the story and the verse agree. Dreaming is a real quarter of the self, a whole world made by the mind. And it still isn't the deepest self, because what's in it can frighten and grieve. That's the teaching. You are not only the one who acts by day, and not only the one who dreams by night. Many Hindu teachers name a witness of both, the sakshi, the one who sees, and the path is learning to stand there. Today, nobody has to be asleep to dream. A fight replayed at three in the morning. A worst case that hasn't happened. A feed that pulls you in. A world lit from within, and it feels completely real. Indra's question still works: is this the deepest me, or something I'm watching?
screen: `THE DREAMER STILL WEEPS.` · `TAIJASA: THE SHINING ONE.` · `U: BETWEEN WAKING AND SLEEP.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · then, large: `IS THIS THE DEEPEST ME?`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let an image come, a place you love, a face, a color, and notice there's no outer light, yet you can see it: that's the shining one, lighting a world from inside. Let it fade and another come, and watch them the way you'd watch a dream, without getting pulled in. Then let them all go, and notice what was watching.
The Mandukya Upanishad. The second quarter is taijasa, the shining one: the dream state, knowing inward, lit from within.
Your line: the dreamer isn't the deepest self. Even the shining one can weep. Two hundred fifty-five days now.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the Mandukya and Gaudapada's Karika are studied together; the comparison between dreaming and waking is a classic subject of that study.

fork.reveal: Indra wanted a self beyond sorrow. the dreamer, lit from within, still grieves, so he turned back.

original.note: Sanskrit: svapna, dream, sleep; Mandukya 4: the dream state is the field of taijasa.
